name: Bento
tagline: Email marketing, behavioral tracking, segmentation, and automation

pricing.native: Pricing varies with contacts and sending
pricing.notes: The pricing model is not safely comparable as one fixed monthly USD amount. Review the official source before publication.

tiers.name: Marketing Platform
tiers.limits: Up to 5,000 active users included; unlimited marketing sends; team seats included.
tiers.notes: Overage pricing applies above 5,000 active users.

tiers.name: Transactional Email Free
tiers.notes: Transactional email is separate from marketing platform pricing.

tiers.name: Transactional Email
tiers.limits: Up to 12,500 transactional emails/month; then $0.09 per 1,000 emails.

tiers.name: Bento Chat add-on
tiers.limits: Chat add-on; numeric usage caps not published in pricing text.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free marketing tier; 30-day trial; transactional email includes first 100 emails free.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly only public pricing; no annual plan verified
pricing.hiddenCosts: Marketing active-user overages: $0.01/user for 5,001-50,000, $0.009 for 50,001-250,000, $0.008 for 250,001+; transactional overage $0.09/1,000 emails.

verdictSummary: The visible email + customer data loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Bento earns its keep through deliverability, reputation, network, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a small email + customer data editor and subscriber database that exports clean HTML and sends only through a reputable user-supplied email provider.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: transactional or bulk email provider key in .env
whatYouLose: sender reputation, deliverability, and suppression handling
whyPeopleStillPay: Bento: The editor is trivial compared with inbox placement, compliance, reputation, unsubscribe handling, analytics, and audience growth infrastructure.
ongoingBurden: Own consent records, suppression lists, bounces, complaints, DNS, templates, accessibility, segmentation, and privacy requests.

priorArt.name: listmonk
priorArt.desc: High-performance self-hosted newsletter and mailing-list manager.

alternatives.name: Dittofeed
alternatives.desc: Event-driven segments and multichannel journeys with a marketer-facing UI; the infrastructure diagram is not decorative.

facts.install: Dittofeed Cloud or Docker Compose/Kubernetes self-host
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted identity and configuration data lives in PostgreSQL and event/segment data in ClickHouse; optional blob data can use object storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Dittofeed handles event-driven segments and journeys, but its Postgres-and-ClickHouse operating burden and narrower all-in-one analytics experience are worse than Bento's managed stack.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker Compose brings Postgres and ClickHouse, but the harder first step is instrumenting product events and connecting an email provider.

alternatives.name: Loops Free
alternatives.desc: Hosted lifecycle email with events and automation for 1,000 contacts; advanced data work still needs another tool.

facts.dataFormat: Contacts, custom properties, events, workflows, and message history live in Loops' cloud; contacts can be imported/exported as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: Loops Free is simple and event-aware, but its free contact/send ceilings and lighter advanced segmentation and data tooling cannot match Bento's behavioral-marketing depth.
facts.setupBlocker: You must authenticate a sending domain and instrument your app or API before lifecycle emails become useful.

alternatives.name: Mautic
alternatives.desc: Behavior tracking, segments and campaigns with years of battle scars; operating it is also a campaign.

alternatives.name: Notifuse
alternatives.desc: Contact events, segments and branching automations in a modern self-hosted app; behavioral plumbing is still yours.

facts.install: Notifuse Cloud signup or self-host with Docker
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted contact, campaign, event, and analytics data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded assets use S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Notifuse supports contacts, events, segments, and branching automations, but you still have to build the behavioral event plumbing and it offers less mature analysis than Bento.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs Docker, PostgreSQL, object storage, a public domain, and a separately configured SMTP or email API provider.

alternatives.name: Plunk
alternatives.desc: Events, conditions and automated email in one open platform; analytics are leaner than Bento's.

facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted data lives in PostgreSQL, queues in Redis, and uploads in bundled MinIO or another S3-compatible store.
facts.gapVsPaid: Plunk can react to events and run conditional email workflows, but its behavioral analytics and segmentation are substantially leaner than Bento's.
facts.setupBlocker: The self-host path needs Docker, several subdomains, DNS/TLS, and an AWS SES account with credentials and domain verification.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Bento is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Bento, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + PostgreSQL.
Primary job: Build a small email + customer data editor and subscriber database that exports clean HTML and sends only through a reputable user-supplied email provider.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: sender reputation and deliverability operations; bounce, complaint, and suppression handling; large-scale segmentation and automation.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
